description: We are a team of enthusiastic young learners with a shared passion for space exploration, science, technology and innovation. We are curious about the universe, fascinated by space missions and excited about understanding the challenges astronauts face during space exploration. Through the NASA Space Ops Challenge, we hope to challenge ourselves, apply our scientific knowledge and experience the excitement of thinking like real astronauts and space scientists.
summary:
We developed Mission Tara-1, a browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer in which the player sits in the Flight Director’s chair and leads a full crewed Moon mission. It has five parts: launching from a real site after a GO / NO-GO poll, travelling 384,000 km to the Moon, landing at the Sea of Tranquility, keeping a four-person south pole base alive for seven days in 3D, and flying the crew home to splashdown.

It addresses the challenge by training young players the way real astronauts train: through hands-on simulation. Every part uses real physics and real NASA data, offers three difficulty levels for different ages, scores each decision, and ends with lessons from real missions such as Apollo 11 and Chandrayaan-3.

It is important because it shows students that spaceflight depends on teamwork, checking and careful decisions, and it makes science and maths exciting. The game is free, runs in any browser with no install or log-in, and works on ordinary school computers, so any classroom can use it.
details:
Our project is a simple Junior Astronaut Trainer which involves many tasks that the 'Junior Astronaut ' has to complete . Our project lets you sit in The Flight Director's chair to check the rocket,count it down,fly it to orbit,cross 384,000km of space,land on the Moon, keep a moon base alive , and fly the crew home again .Every number comes from real rockets and real missions. What does it do or how does it work?
Mission Tara-1 is a browser game that puts the player in the Flight Director’s chair for a full crewed Moon mission, in five parts:

  1. Launch: pick a real launch site (Sriharikota, Kennedy, Kourou or Baikonur), run a GO / NO-GO poll across six stations to catch hidden problems, then fly the rocket to orbit by hand.
  2. Travel: burn out of Earth orbit, cross 384,000 km in a 3-day cruise with obstacles, and brake into Moon orbit.
  3. Landing: pilot the lander down to the Sea of Tranquility, handling a 1202 program alarm, a boulder field and low fuel, as Apollo 11 did.
  4. Moon base (3D): keep a 4-person base near the south pole alive for 7 days by managing air, water, food, power, radiation, a solar storm and the radio delay to Earth.
  5. Return: burn for home, correct course, re-enter and splash down.

Each part runs on a physics simulation, scores the player, and ends with lessons from real missions. A built-in assistant called TARA answers questions about the game and spaceflight.

What benefits does it have?

  • Players learn by doing: for example, a launch site nearer the equator gets more free speed from Earth’s spin, and fuel saved at launch carries into the trip to the Moon.
  • Three difficulty levels (Cadet, Pilot, Commander) let beginners and confident players both enjoy it.
  • Failure teaches: every crash or abort explains what went wrong and what real engineers did about it.
  • It is one file that opens in any browser, with no install and no log-in needed.

What is the intended impact?
We want young students to see that spaceflight is about teamwork, checking, and careful decisions, not only the rocket. We hope it builds curiosity about science and maths, shows Indian missions like Chandrayaan-3 alongside Apollo and Artemis, and gives teachers a free tool that works on ordinary school computers.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Graphics: HTML Canvas for the 2D parts, and three.js (WebGL) with bloom effects for the 3D Moon base.
  • Maps: D3 (d3-geo, d3-array) and TopoJSON with a world map for the rotating globe.
  • Sound: Web Audio API for synthesised effects, and the browser’s speech voice for mission control.
  • Storage: the browser’s local storage for scores and optional crew accounts.
  • Data: NASA sources such as DONKI solar flare records, the life support baseline values, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and LCROSS findings, and Apollo mission records.
  • AI: Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, was used for touch-ups at the end of the game.
  • Hardware: no special hardware, only a computer or tablet with a modern browser.

How is your project creative?

  • It covers the whole journey in one connected story, so choices early on affect later parts.
  • All the art and sound is generated in code: Earth, the Moon, stars, smoke, rocket roar and radio beeps, with no image or audio files.
  • It turns real moments into gameplay, such as the Apollo 11 alarm and the 1.3-second radio delay.
  • The Moon base mission turns real NASA numbers into a survival challenge.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy: every real number is listed with its source, and simplified “game values” are labelled as such. Recorded data is never shown as live.
  • Age and skill: simple language, guidance arrows on Easy, and short sessions (a 7-day base mission fits in about 8 minutes).
  • Access: works by keyboard and touch, includes screen reader labels and a reduced motion option, and keeps working if sound is blocked.
  • Privacy: accounts are optional, stay on the device, and passwords are salted and hashed.
  • Honesty(SI):We state our use of SI for our project during the hackathon but we used SI only for touch-ups at the end of the game
